title: Bluebook Introductory Citation Signals: A Graded Taxonomy of Degree-of-Support

extracted.subtask_short: Grading citation signal strength and direction
extracted.subtask_description: Encodes, via a controlled vocabulary of introductory signal words placed before a legal citation, exactly how strongly and in what direction a cited authority supports or contradicts the proposition it follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: No signal - direct, unambiguous support
rubrics_metrics.description: Used when the authority 'directly states the proposition,' provides a direct quotation, or is itself the source being identified in the text. This is the strongest possible support signal: no signal at all is required precisely because the source-to-claim mapping is unambiguous and direct.

rubrics_metrics.name: E.g. - direct support via one of several examples
rubrics_metrics.description: The cited authority states the proposition, and citing other authorities that also state it would be unhelpful/redundant. Direct support, explicitly flagged as merely one of several available equally-direct examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accord - direct corroborating support from multiple sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Used (typically after a quotation or explicit statement from one jurisdiction/authority) to cite additional authorities that also directly state the same proposition - direct, corroborating support from multiple sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: See - indirect support requiring an inferential step
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The cited authority clearly supports a proposition but there is an inferential step between the proposition as stated and the cited authority.' This is the single most common signal and is the explicit legal-citation term for what the medical/NLP literature calls 'partial support' or requires 'interpretation' to connect - the source doesn't say the claim verbatim, but a reader can clearly derive the claim from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: See also - supplementary corroborating support
rubrics_metrics.description: Cites additional/supplementary authority supporting a proposition already supported by a preceding See or [no signal] citation; requires an explanatory parenthetical stating the relevance of the extra material. Functions as corroborating-but-secondary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cf. - analogous support by comparison, not directly on point
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduces a source that supports a different but sufficiently analogous proposition, such that it indirectly supports the stated proposition by analogy. A citation can be a legitimate, honest citation while still not being directly on-point - it supports a structurally similar claim, and the burden is on the reader/author to draw the analogy explicitly (a required parenthetical typically explains the analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare ... with ... - illustrative comparison support
rubrics_metrics.description: A comparison between two or more sources is offered as illustrating or supporting the proposition (e.g., contrasting two cases whose difference in outcome illustrates the point); also requires an explanatory parenthetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contra - direct contradiction, no inferential gap
rubrics_metrics.description: The cited authority 'directly states a contradictory proposition' - the direct-contradiction analog of [no signal], i.e., maximally strong disagreement with no inferential gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: But see - indirect contradiction requiring an inferential step
rubrics_metrics.description: The cited authority 'clearly supports a proposition contradictory to the textual assertion,' but (mirroring See) with an inferential step required to get from the source to the contradiction - the indirect-contradiction analog of See.

rubrics_metrics.name: But cf. - analogous contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: An authority that is 'analogously contradictory' - supports, by analogy, a proposition that conflicts with the stated one. The contradiction-side analog of Cf.

rubrics_metrics.name: See generally - background only, no support/contradiction claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Cited for background/context reading; explicitly does not claim to directly support or refute the specific proposition, only to provide useful related context. Requires an explanatory parenthetical. This is the legal-citation equivalent of scite.ai's 'mentioning' category - a citation present in the text but making no explicit support/contradiction claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required explanatory parenthetical for non-strongest-tier signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Every signal beyond the strongest tier (See also, Cf., Compare...with, But cf., See generally) formally requires an explanatory parenthetical - the citing author must, in the citation itself, articulate why the source counts as supporting/contradicting/relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'show your work' requirement is a useful design principle for any claim-matching pipeline: a good claim-citation-support judgment should come with a stated reason, not just a categorical label.
